title: When It Comes to a Critical Choice, Ask an Equally Critical Question
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece shows how complex, repeated decisions can often be reduced to a short set of critical yes-or-no questions, using emergency-room triage and Warren Buffett's investment criteria as two very different examples. University of California statisticians distilled heart-attack risk assessment into three simple questions about blood pressure, age, and heart rate; Buffett reportedly uses three questions of his own to evaluate a potential investment. The author argues that any leader facing a recurring, high-stakes choice -- from sales territory assignment to lineup selection -- can eventually distill their own experience and data into one or two defining questions. The piece ends by turning the idea back on the reader, asking what questions they should be using to guide their own repeated decisions.
points: Complex, repetitive decisions can often be reduced to a short set of critical questions.
Statisticians reduced heart-attack risk triage to three simple diagnostic questions.
Warren Buffett reportedly uses three questions to evaluate whether to invest in a business.
Leaders can build their own critical questions from accumulated experience and data.
quotes: This critical decision influences treatment and has a profound impact on whether a patient survives or not.
By answering any of these three critical questions in the affirmative, any doctor can reach a quality decision regarding immediate and high risk.
Consequential choice decisions that are repetitive in nature can normally be boiled down into one or more critical questions that streamline the decision.
Here’s an all-too-common episode that unfortunately plays out every day somewhere.
A patient suspecting a heart attack is rushed to a hospital for emergency care.
The attending physician must quickly decide whether the sufferer should be treated as a high-risk or low-risk patient.
Yet, there are so many factors to consider, many of which have to do with a patient’s history.
Too often, the patient is either inaccurate about these factors or is not able to communicate clearly.
